nodeData.note: The national picture, region by region, November 2026.

children.note: Five interlocking problems: an insurgency that still governs the countryside; a constitutional crisis that has turned into armed clashes; a security transition (AU out, Somalis in) that is under-funded; a return of piracy tied to the wider Red Sea / Iran war; and foreign powers backing rival Somali camps.

nodeData.note: Five interlocking problems: an insurgency that still governs the countryside; a constitutional crisis that has turned into armed clashes; a security transition (AU out, Somalis in) that is under-funded; a return of piracy tied to the wider Red Sea / Iran war; and foreign powers backing rival Somali camps.

children.note: Al-Qaeda affiliate; still controls or governs much of the countryside in south and central Somalia, taxes trade, runs courts. The 2022–23 government offensive stalled; 2025 saw a counter-offensive in Middle/Lower Shabelle and Hirshabelle.
IEDs, ambushes, complex attacks on bases, economic coercion. Joint AU-UN-FGS assessment (May 2026) warns territorial gains can be reversed without stabilisation, governance presence and logistics.

children.topic: Towns at risk as AU shrinks
children.note: Crisis Group (Sep 2026) names Qoryoley (Lower Shabelle) and Jalalaqsi (Hirshabelle) as towns that could fall if AU contingents leave without replacements. Several positions handed to Somali forces earlier were later lost.
Operations against al-Shabaab slow sharply during political crises, letting the group recover and regroup — the pattern seen again in 2026.
Documented ties with Yemen's Houthis (weapons, training reported); the Gulf of Aden trade network connects al-Shabaab, Houthis, AQAP elements and pirate financiers.
Taxation of roads, ports and businesses; control of transport routes and economic centres would add revenue if towns fall.

Puntland sits at the centre of three of Somalia's security problems at once: the ISIS-Somalia campaign in the Cal Miskaad mountains, the 2026 piracy surge off its east coast, and the political standoff with Mogadishu. It has suspended relations with the federal government, allied with Somaliland against the new North East State, and runs its own security forces.

Bari region mountains host the Islamic State's regional finance office (al-Karrar) — a money and logistics node for IS across Africa. Puntland's campaign since Dec 2024, with US and UAE air support, cleared many camps but the group persists in the ranges and in Bosaso cells.
Planned, led and paid for by Puntland; the federal army has no role. Effective, but proof that the national architecture does not reach the north.
Recruits from Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Morocco, Yemen and beyond; UN Panel of Experts (Nov 2025) tracks its finance role.

Puntland suspended ties over the constitutional process (2024) and rejected the March 2026 amendments; military standoff with federal-aligned units since mid-June 2026; Puntland seized three FGS-aligned bases in Aug 2026 and now controls all security forces on its territory.

Mogadishu created North East State (2025) in territory Puntland claims (Sool–Sanaag–Cayn area contested with Somaliland). Result: a Puntland–Somaliland alliance against the federal government, despite their own old dispute over Las Anod.

Three of the six 2026 hijackings happened off Puntland's east coast; all hijacked ships are held off the Puntland coast. Pirate kingpins never left — some linked to Puntland or federal security circles. Mogadishu condemned the surge "off the coast of Puntland" (6 Sep 2026).
IUU foreign fishing, aid cuts, rising food and fuel prices, little state presence on the coast — the same conditions as 2008–2012.
Puntland's own coast guard (built with UAE support since 2010) — the only serious counter-piracy force on land; its funding and command are entangled in the UAE–Mogadishu rift.

Puntland rejected Mogadishu's Jan 2026 cancellation of UAE defence agreements; Emirati firms run Bosaso port (P&O/DP World), the UAE trains and pays Puntland forces and backed the ISIS campaign from the air.

children.topic: What Puntland needs from a national deal
children.note: Recognition of its security role in the architecture, a share of federal and donor security funding, an agreed status for North East State, and a coast-guard mandate for the maritime zone — none of which a Mogadishu-centred settlement currently offers.

March 2026: Parliament amended chapters 5–15 of the provisional constitution and extended terms from 4 to 5 years; President Hassan Sheikh signed 8 March. His mandate was due to end 15 May 2026; opposition (Somali Future Council: Puntland, Jubaland leaders, former presidents) rejects the extension. US/UK-facilitated talks in May ended in stalemate. Electoral commission now says polls April–May 2027; opposition rejects that too.
Fighting in Mogadishu and around Baidoa (South West State) with drones and reportedly fighter jets; federal forces took Baidoa, Laftagareen resigned, interim president appointed by Mogadishu.
Puntland, Jubaland, then South West suspended relations with Mogadishu. Puntland–FGS military standoff since June 2026; Puntland seized FGS-aligned bases in Aug 2026.
New FGS-aligned state (2025) squeezed between Puntland and Somaliland; pushed Puntland and Somaliland into an alliance.
No unified national security structure can be built while FGS and member states are at war politically; the election dispute complicates planning for the AU drawdown.

National Security Architecture (2017, revised 2023): SNA ~18 brigades on paper, Danab commandos (US-trained), Gorgor (Turkish-trained), NISA intelligence, Somali Police, Custodial Corps, plus state forces (Darwish). Reality: command still fragmented between federal and state lines; clan balance unresolved.

Mogadishu said in Aug 2026 that about 14,000 Somali troops were available for operations — far fewer than the paper strength, and lighter on equipment, air, intelligence and logistics than foreign units.
Operations rely on foreign intelligence, air power, transport and logistics; one-for-one replacement of AU positions is called a "hazardous proposition".
Gorgor (Turkey, TURKSOM camp since 2017) and Danab (US) are the most capable; both tied to bilateral partners, not a single national chain.
Effective locally, but answer to state presidents who are now in opposition to Mogadishu.

UN Special Rapporteur (2026): counter-terrorism strategy not shared, weak oversight and accountability; effectiveness impeded by clan divisions and centre–state fragmentation. First UN human-rights host-country agreement signed 6 May 2026.

AU Support and Stabilisation Mission (replaced ATMIS, Jan 2025). Resolution 2809 (23 Dec 2025) authorises it to 31 Dec 2026. Deployed at 49 locations vs 23 planned — kept because of the risk of vacuums. UN logistics (UNSOS) extended 12 months by the US; drawdown now expected from Jan 2027; replacement system could start H2 2027.
Persistent shortfalls hit aviation, engineering and mobility. EU added €75m (Apr 2026). US opposes using UN assessed contributions (res. 2719). Pledging conference proposed.

Likely replacement: bilateral deals with Uganda (Mogadishu area), Kenya and Ethiopia (near their borders); Burundi and Djibouti may struggle to stay. Turkey central through training and deployments; US continues CT strikes.
Crisis Group: prioritise holding existing territory over new offensives; coordinate with partners who protects which town, road and infrastructure.
UNTMIS left 31 Oct 2026; future UN political engagement unclear (possibly via the Horn of Africa special envoy).

Since late April 2026 six commercial ships hijacked (vs three in the previous 14 years); four held with 60+ seafarers (Sep 2026). Two zones: Puntland's east coast (Garacad–Durdura) and the Yemeni side of the Gulf of Aden. Four of six were tankers; none had armed guards.

Warships pulled to Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb during the US–Israel war on Iran; more ships re-routing past Somalia; high oil prices; calm seas; industry complacency after the High Risk Area was lifted (2023).
Unconfirmed reports of Houthi training, equipment and financing; launches from Yemeni settlements; Yemeni nationals involved. A way to disrupt shipping without drawing a military response.
Coastal Puntland under-served, aid cuts, IUU fishing, rising food and fuel prices; pirate kingpins never left — some linked to Puntland or federal security circles.

Trafficking–piracy–extremism ecology across the Gulf of Aden: Houthis, al-Shabaab, AQAP elements, pirates sharing financiers and captains. Mogadishu to raise piracy at the UN Security Council (Sep 2026).

Two fluid blocs in the Horn: Egypt–Saudi–Turkey (with Sudan's army, Eritrea) vs UAE–Israel (with Ethiopia). Turkey backs the federal government; the UAE keeps ties with Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland. Somali elites court outsiders with ports, corridors and bases.
Training camp since 2017, strategic agreements since 2024, naval and oil-gas deals; Turkish jets reportedly involved near Baidoa (unconfirmed).
Jan 2026: Mogadishu annulled all defence and security agreements with the UAE; UAE keeps port interests and direct ties with the three northern/southern administrations.
Somalia signed defence agreements with Saudi Arabia and Qatar after the UAE break, with Turkish and Egyptian support; Egyptian troops in AUSSOM.
26 Dec 2025: first UN member to recognise Somaliland; Somaliland ambassador in Israel (May 2026). Condemned by Mogadishu; Houthis threatened any Israeli presence.
Ethiopia–Somaliland port/recognition MoU (2024) strained relations; Ethiopia remains a troop contributor and will likely hold forces near its border; war has returned to Tigray.
Bilateral counter-terrorism strikes continue; extended UNSOS funding by a year; co-facilitated FGS–opposition talks with the UK.
The questions a specialist would track.
An inclusive agreement on constitution, electoral model and interim arrangements before April–May 2027 — or deeper FGS vs Puntland/Jubaland/South West conflict with foreign drones.
Which of the 49 locations are handed over, to whom, and whether towns like Qoryoley and Jalalaqsi hold.
Whether a pledging conference or EU/Gulf money closes the gap; US position on res. 2719.
Naval presence off Puntland, armed guards and BMP compliance, prosecution and ransom policy, Houthi links.
Standoff, seized bases, ISIS-Somalia campaign continuing without federal support.
Displacement, aid cuts, drought/food prices — the ground conditions that feed recruitment and piracy.

children.topic: 9 · A settlement all Somalis gain from
children.note: The threads above point the same way: no region can be secure alone. What the sources converge on as the shared path, Mogadishu to Bosaso to Kismayo.

Constitution, electoral model and interim arrangements agreed with all member states and the opposition, with a realistic timetable — the precondition for everything else (Chatham House, Crisis Group).

children.topic: A security architecture that includes the states
children.note: Puntland, Jubaland and the others inside the planning for the AU drawdown, with agreed roles, funding shares and a joint FGS–states–partners forum deciding who holds which town, road and port.
Keep what is held; follow every clearance with governance, services and courts so towns do not fall back — the gains most at risk are in the south, the lessons come from Puntland's own campaign.

children.topic: Coast and sea as one system
children.note: Coast-guard capacity (Puntland Maritime Police Force, a national coast guard), fisheries protection against IUU fleets, livelihoods on the coast, and a coordinated international naval presence — benefits every port from Berbera to Kismayo.
Many partners (Turkey, Gulf states, US, EU, AU neighbours) but one Somali-owned plan, so foreign rivalries are not fought out through Somali factions.

Al-Shabaab, ISIS-Somalia, pirate financiers and Houthi networks use the same trade routes and the same grievances; intelligence sharing between federal and state forces and the diaspora hits all of them at once.
